A system of linear equations is **consistent** if it has *at least one* solution. Otherwise, it is **inconsistent**.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is **consistent independent**.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is **consistent dependent**.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

Remember that a system is *consistent* if it has a solution. So, the idea that a system of equations with no solution is *inconsistent* probably makes sense to you.

But what about the difference between consistent *dependent* and consistent *independent?* What is the reasoning behind these naming conventions?

To help understand consistent dependent vs. consistent independent, we'll look at some concrete examples:

- First, consider the following system.
${3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4$
This system has *infinitely many* solutions corresponding to the fact that the two lines coincide.![](images/e9/e9e98008aa5972889efdd3af0689da310c69bca06dd410a391a37e22aa8b0098.png)
In a previous lesson, we saw that the set of all solutions $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ can be expressed as
$({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}})$
where ${\color{blue}{x}}$ is any number. Consequently, any ${\color{red}{y}}$-value in our solution is *dependent* on a corresponding ${\color{blue}{x}}$-value. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*dependent*.
- Next, we consider the following system:
${y = 2x + 1; y = 1 - x$
This system has a single solution corresponding to the unique intersection point of the two lines.![](images/bd/bd7edb530e16b853318a3e38785c7b6353c1b54f10ee3c4e2de7da915450f6d9.png)
The unique solution $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ is given by the single point $({\color{blue}{0}},{\color{red}{1}})$. In this case, the components of the solution do not depend on $x$ or $y$. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*independent*.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider a system of two linear equations with two variables, where each equation is represented by the corresponding straight line in the plane. What can we say about the intersections of these lines, given that the system is

1. inconsistent,
2. consistent independent, or
3. consistent dependent?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

In other words, we have the following cases:

- If a system is *inconsistent* (has no solutions), the corresponding lines are parallel (do not intersect). And vice versa, parallel lines correspond to an inconsistent system.
- If a system is *consistent independent* (i.e., has exactly one solution), the corresponding lines intersect at exactly one point. And vice versa, intersecting lines correspond to a consistent independent system.
- If a system is *consistent dependent* (i.e., has infinitely many solutions), the corresponding lines intersect at infinitely many points (coincide). And vice versa, coinciding lines correspond to a consistent dependent system.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Determine whether the following system of equations is consistent or inconsistent. If it is consistent, indicate whether it is consistent dependent or consistent independent.
${x - 2y - 2 = 0; 4x - 8y = 8$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A system of equations is *consistent* if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, it is called *inconsistent*.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is called *consistent independent*.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is called *consistent dependent*.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

We will solve the system using substitution.

First, we can solve the first equation for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y - 2 &= 0 \\
x &= 2 + 2y
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute

$$
x=2+2y
$$

into the second equation to obtain an equation that we can solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x - 8y &= 8 \\
4(2 + 2y) - 8y &= 8 \\
8 + 8y - 8y &= 8 \\
8 &= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the system is consistent dependent.

We will solve the system using substitution.

First, we can solve the first equation for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x - 3y &= -9 \\ -2x &= -9 + 3y \\ x &= \frac{9}{2} - \frac{3}{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=\frac{9}{2} - \frac{3}{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

into the second equation to obtain an equation that we can solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x - 3y &= -9 \\ -2\left(\frac{9}{2} - \frac{3}{2}y\right) - 3y &= -9 \\ -9 + 3y - 3y &= -9 \\ -9 &= -9\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the system is consistent dependent.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the following system of equations.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-4x + 3y &=3 \\ 2x + 4y &=-24\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system of equations is {{field-1}}.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A system of equations is *consistent* if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, it is called *inconsistent*.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is called *consistent independent*.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

First, we can solve the first equation for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x + 3y &= 3 \\ -4x &= 3 - 3y \\ x &= -\frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4}y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute

$$
\begin{aligned}x&=-\frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4}y\end{aligned}
$$

into the second equation to obtain an equation that we can solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x + 4y &= -24 \\ 2\left(-\frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4}y\right) + 4y &= -24 \\ -\frac{3}{2} + \frac{3}{2}y + 4y &= -24 \\ \frac{11}{2}y &= -\frac{45}{2} \\ y &= -\frac{45}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a single value of $y$, and $x$ is determined by $x=-\frac{3}{4} + \frac{3}{4}y$, there is exactly one solution to the system. Therefore, the system is consistent independent.

Determine whether the following system of equations is consistent or inconsistent. If it is consistent, indicate whether it is consistent dependent or consistent independent.
${x - 2y - 2 = 0; 4x - 8y = 8$

A system of equations is *consistent* if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, it is called *inconsistent*.

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is called *consistent independent*.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is called *consistent dependent*.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

We will solve the system using substitution.

First, we can solve the first equation for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y - 2 &= 0 \\
x &= 2 + 2y
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute

$$
x=2+2y
$$

into the second equation to obtain an equation that we can solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x - 8y &= 8 \\
4(2 + 2y) - 8y &= 8 \\
8 + 8y - 8y &= 8 \\
8 &= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the system is consistent dependent.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
A system of linear equations is **consistent** if it has *at least one* solution. Otherwise, it is **inconsistent**.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is **consistent independent**.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is **consistent dependent**.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

Remember that a system is *consistent* if it has a solution. So, the idea that a system of equations with no solution is *inconsistent* probably makes sense to you.

But what about the difference between consistent *dependent* and consistent *independent?* What is the reasoning behind these naming conventions?

To help understand consistent dependent vs. consistent independent, we'll look at some concrete examples:

- First, consider the following system.
${3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4$
This system has *infinitely many* solutions corresponding to the fact that the two lines coincide.![](images/e9/e9e98008aa5972889efdd3af0689da310c69bca06dd410a391a37e22aa8b0098.png)
In a previous lesson, we saw that the set of all solutions $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ can be expressed as
$({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}})$
where ${\color{blue}{x}}$ is any number. Consequently, any ${\color{red}{y}}$-value in our solution is *dependent* on a corresponding ${\color{blue}{x}}$-value. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*dependent*.
- Next, we consider the following system:
${y = 2x + 1; y = 1 - x$
This system has a single solution corresponding to the unique intersection point of the two lines.![](images/bd/bd7edb530e16b853318a3e38785c7b6353c1b54f10ee3c4e2de7da915450f6d9.png)
The unique solution $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ is given by the single point $({\color{blue}{0}},{\color{red}{1}})$. In this case, the components of the solution do not depend on $x$ or $y$. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*independent*.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider a system of two linear equations with two variables, where each equation is represented by the corresponding straight line in the plane. What can we say about the intersections of these lines, given that the system is

1. inconsistent,
2. consistent independent, or
3. consistent dependent?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

In other words, we have the following cases:

- If a system is *inconsistent* (has no solutions), the corresponding lines are parallel (do not intersect). And vice versa, parallel lines correspond to an inconsistent system.
- If a system is *consistent independent* (i.e., has exactly one solution), the corresponding lines intersect at exactly one point. And vice versa, intersecting lines correspond to a consistent independent system.
- If a system is *consistent dependent* (i.e., has infinitely many solutions), the corresponding lines intersect at infinitely many points (coincide). And vice versa, coinciding lines correspond to a consistent dependent system.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Determine whether the following system of equations is consistent or inconsistent. If it is consistent, indicate whether it is consistent dependent or consistent independent.
${x - 2y - 2 = 0; 4x - 8y = 8$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A system of equations is *consistent* if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, it is called *inconsistent*.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is called *consistent independent*.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is called *consistent dependent*.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

We will solve the system using substitution.

First, we can solve the first equation for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y - 2 &= 0 \\
x &= 2 + 2y
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute

$$
x=2+2y
$$

into the second equation to obtain an equation that we can solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x - 8y &= 8 \\
4(2 + 2y) - 8y &= 8 \\
8 + 8y - 8y &= 8 \\
8 &= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the system is consistent dependent.

Remember that a system is *consistent* if it has a solution. So, the idea that a system of equations with no solution is *inconsistent* probably makes sense to you.

But what about the difference between consistent *dependent* and consistent *independent?* What is the reasoning behind these naming conventions?

To help understand consistent dependent vs. consistent independent, we'll look at some concrete examples:

- First, consider the following system.
${3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4$
This system has *infinitely many* solutions corresponding to the fact that the two lines coincide.![](images/e9/e9e98008aa5972889efdd3af0689da310c69bca06dd410a391a37e22aa8b0098.png)
In a previous lesson, we saw that the set of all solutions $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ can be expressed as
$({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}})$
where ${\color{blue}{x}}$ is any number. Consequently, any ${\color{red}{y}}$-value in our solution is *dependent* on a corresponding ${\color{blue}{x}}$-value. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*dependent*.
- Next, we consider the following system:
${y = 2x + 1; y = 1 - x$
This system has a single solution corresponding to the unique intersection point of the two lines.![](images/bd/bd7edb530e16b853318a3e38785c7b6353c1b54f10ee3c4e2de7da915450f6d9.png)
The unique solution $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$ is given by the single point $({\color{blue}{0}},{\color{red}{1}})$. In this case, the components of the solution do not depend on $x$ or $y$. Thus, the system of equations is consistent-*independent*.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider a system of two linear equations with two variables, where each equation is represented by the corresponding straight line in the plane. What can we say about the intersections of these lines, given that the system is

1. inconsistent,
2. consistent independent, or
3. consistent dependent?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The solutions of a linear system with two variables correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines defined by the equations. Three possibilities exist, as shown below.

![](images/8c/8c544df38ce82dd70c3d01718233c9fae1fae0534748892643a12b6556918fb7.png)

In other words, we have the following cases:

- If a system is *inconsistent* (has no solutions), the corresponding lines are parallel (do not intersect). And vice versa, parallel lines correspond to an inconsistent system.
- If a system is *consistent independent* (i.e., has exactly one solution), the corresponding lines intersect at exactly one point. And vice versa, intersecting lines correspond to a consistent independent system.
- If a system is *consistent dependent* (i.e., has infinitely many solutions), the corresponding lines intersect at infinitely many points (coincide). And vice versa, coinciding lines correspond to a consistent dependent system.

17592186198220.:question/problem:
Determine whether the following system of equations is consistent or inconsistent. If it is consistent, indicate whether it is consistent dependent or consistent independent.
${x - 2y - 2 = 0; 4x - 8y = 8$
17592186198220.:question/worked-solution:
A system of equations is *consistent* if it has at least one solution. Otherwise, it is called *inconsistent*.

Consistent systems, in turn, can be of the following two types:

- When a system of equations has a *single* solution, it is called *consistent independent*.
- When a system of equations has an *infinite number* of solutions, it is called *consistent dependent*.

We can summarize these definitions using the diagram shown below.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

We will solve the system using substitution.

First, we can solve the first equation for $x$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y - 2 &= 0 \\
x &= 2 + 2y
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we can substitute

$$
x=2+2y
$$

into the second equation to obtain an equation that we can solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x - 8y &= 8 \\
4(2 + 2y) - 8y &= 8 \\
8 + 8y - 8y &= 8 \\
8 &= 8
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the system is consistent dependent.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$
![](images/67/673ea82819858b9a46e0e351a8d6f41b069ed039ee0d31a382110f938f7ef72a.svg)

We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at

![](images/35/35627a034b30736abb057c01f3251fc047dce780a8cbcf389f8b5c2c2317d766.svg)

This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

![](images/32/32a252e05e299a206f2f3776a2a04419f21726e1f8f542cfd4f328dac3251f21.svg)

Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

![](images/b3/b3512e604d6c4246c5582a75360076115c4bd9b6701c42587f318254b1c026a3.svg)

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now
![](images/76/765eafb8a8b60aec9af512eeb666e2e13dbf83b8bc331b6effa75143930b4892.svg)

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix}.

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=19 \\ y+2z &=13 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+2(5)=13\,⟹\,y=13-10=3.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=3$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(3)+2(5)=19\,⟹\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=6,y=3$, and $z=5.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨6,3,5⟩.$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=8$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 17\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=1 \\ y-3z &=-9 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-3(1)=-9\,⟹\,y=-6.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-6$ and $z=1$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x-(-6)+2(1)=1\,⟹\,x=-7.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-7,y=-6$, and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨-7,-6,1⟩.$

Consider the system of linear equations

$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=1 \\ y &=4 \\ z &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=4$ and $z=-4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(4)+2(-4)=1\,⟹\,x=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=5,y=4$, and $z=-4.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨5,4,-4⟩.$

$$

$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=8 \\ y-z &=1 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(5) &=1\,⟹\,y=6.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(6)+2(5) &=8\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}

Thus, the solution is $x=4$, $y=6$, and $z=5.$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -3 & -6 & 4 & -8 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y-z &=4 \\ y+2z &=-2 \\ z &=4,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=4$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2(4) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-10$ and $z=4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2(-10)-(4) &=4\,⟹\,x=28.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=28$, $y=-10$, and $z=4.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}5 & 20 & -10 & -5 \\ -2 & -8 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}5 & 20 & -10 & -5 \\ -2 & -8 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & -8 & 6 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply the $2$nd row by $\frac{1}{3}$ and the $3$rd row by $\frac{1}{2}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+6y-3z &=-1 \\ -2x-12y+8z &=1 \\ -x-5y+4z &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ -2 & -12 & 8 & 1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ -2 & -12 & 8 & 1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply the $3$rd row by $\frac{1}{2}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

![](images/b3/b3512e604d6c4246c5582a75360076115c4bd9b6701c42587f318254b1c026a3.svg)

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now
![](images/76/765eafb8a8b60aec9af512eeb666e2e13dbf83b8bc331b6effa75143930b4892.svg)

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=19 \\ y+2z &=13 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+2(5)=13\,⟹\,y=13-10=3.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=3$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(3)+2(5)=19\,⟹\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=6,y=3$, and $z=5.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨6,3,5⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-3 \\ y-2z &=-2 \\ z &=8,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=8$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-2(8)=-2\,⟹\,y=-2+16=14.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=14$ and $z=8$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2(14)+(8)=-3\,⟹\,x=17.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=17,y=14$, and $z=8.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨17,14,8⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=6 \\ y+z &=5 \\ 2x+3y+2z &=14\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=6 \\ y+z &=5 \\ z &=3,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=3$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(3)=5\,⟹\,y=5-3=2.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=2$ and $z=3$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(2)+(3)=6\,⟹\,x=6-5=1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=1,y=2$ and $z=3.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=-3 \\ x+2y+2z &=2 \\ 3x+4y+4z &=8\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 17\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=-3 \\ y &=5 \\ z &=-6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=5$ and $z=-6$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+5+2(-6)=-3\,⟹\,x-7=-3\,⟹\,x=4.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=4,$ $y=5,$ and $z=-6.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=1 \\ 2x+3y+4z &=6 \\ 3x+3y+4z &=11\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 & 4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 3 & 3 & 4 & 11\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=1 \\ y &=4 \\ z &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=4$ and $z=-4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(4)+2(-4)=1\,⟹\,x=5.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=5,y=4$, and $z=-4.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨5,4,-4⟩.$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -11 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(5) &=1\,⟹\,y=6.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(6)+2(5) &=8\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=4$, $y=6$, and $z=5.$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+6y-3z &=-1 \\ -2x-12y+8z &=1 \\ -x-5y+4z &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ -2 & -12 & 8 & 1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ -2 & -12 & 8 & 1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ -1 & -5 & 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we multiply the $3$rd row by $\frac{1}{2}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 6 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -\frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Using Standard Gaussian Elimination with Row Exchanges

17592186049058.:topic/title: Solving 3x3 Systems of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$
![](images/67/673ea82819858b9a46e0e351a8d6f41b069ed039ee0d31a382110f938f7ef72a.svg)

We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at

![](images/35/35627a034b30736abb057c01f3251fc047dce780a8cbcf389f8b5c2c2317d766.svg)

This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:

![](images/32/32a252e05e299a206f2f3776a2a04419f21726e1f8f542cfd4f328dac3251f21.svg)

Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

![](images/b3/b3512e604d6c4246c5582a75360076115c4bd9b6701c42587f318254b1c026a3.svg)

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now
![](images/76/765eafb8a8b60aec9af512eeb666e2e13dbf83b8bc331b6effa75143930b4892.svg)

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=19 \\ y+2z &=13 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+2(5)=13\,⟹\,y=13-10=3.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=3$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(3)+2(5)=19\,⟹\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=6,y=3$, and $z=5.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨6,3,5⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix}.

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-3 \\ y-2z &=-2 \\ z &=8,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=8$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-2(8)=-2\,⟹\,y=-2+16=14.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=14$ and $z=8$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x-2(14)+(8)=-3\,⟹\,x=17.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=17,y=14$, and $z=8.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨17,14,8⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

$$

The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=1,y=2$ and $z=3.$

Consider the system of linear equations

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 17\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=-3 \\ y &=5 \\ z &=-6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=5$ and $z=-6$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+5+2(-6)=-3\,⟹\,x-7=-3\,⟹\,x=4.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=4,$ $y=5,$ and $z=-6.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations
![](images/cd/cd75b39fc76773c0b3938ab6d60651e2b08dcd9ac325cc05718837934130ea07.svg)

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

![](images/93/933b897b7bc067610c87ea50a6fb871f04c5cc4610bd5bb0c868e6ffbac25e86.svg)

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get $a_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$

$$

$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$
![](images/67/673ea82819858b9a46e0e351a8d6f41b069ed039ee0d31a382110f938f7ef72a.svg)

We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

- If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

- We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$

- if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

- If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

- We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely, 

- if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

- If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

- In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now
![](images/76/765eafb8a8b60aec9af512eeb666e2e13dbf83b8bc331b6effa75143930b4892.svg)

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix}.

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=19 \\ y+2z &=13 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+2(5)=13\,⟹\,y=13-10=3.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=3$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(3)+2(5)=19\,⟹\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=6,y=3$, and $z=5.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨6,3,5⟩.$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & -6 & 3 & -9 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ -2 & 5 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & -5 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 8\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y+z &=-3 \\ y-2z &=-2 \\ z &=8,\end{aligned}\right.

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=8$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 & 14\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

The augmented matrix for this system is

$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 17\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

17592186287999.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear equations

\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=-3 \\ x+2y+2z &=2 \\ 3x+4y+4z &=8\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and hence solve the linear system.
17592186287999.:question/worked-solution:
The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 3 & 4 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & 17\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 12\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=-3 \\ y &=5 \\ z &=-6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. Substituting both $y=5$ and $z=-6$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+5+2(-6)=-3\,⟹\,x-7=-3\,⟹\,x=4.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=4,$ $y=5,$ and $z=-6.$

17592186368702.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 3 & -6 & -3 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & -4 & 12 & 36 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=1 \\ y-3z &=-9 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y-3(1)=-9\,⟹\,y=-6.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-6$ and $z=1$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x-(-6)+2(1)=1\,⟹\,x=-7.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-7,y=-6$, and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨-7,-6,1⟩.$

$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=1 \\ y-z &=-4 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ -3 & -6 & 4 & -8 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 7 & -1 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y-z &=4 \\ y+2z &=-2 \\ z &=4,\end{aligned}\right.

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=4$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2(4) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-10.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=-10$ and $z=4$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+2(-10)-(4) &=4\,⟹\,x=28.\end{aligned}

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+z &=1 \\ y-z &=2 \\ z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The augmented matrix for this system can be written as 

$$
M =
	\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & 2 & 1 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -1 & 2 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 3\end{array}
	\right].
$$

Notice that the matrix is in *row echelon form* (or REF). Whenever the augmented matrix is in row echelon form, we can solve the system using a method called **back substitution**.

Back substitution involves

- starting with the lowest equation (which is already solved for one variable),

- substituting the result into the next-lowest equation to find the solution for another variable, and

- continuing to substitute the result into the next-lowest equation until the values of all the variables have been found.

Here, the third equation states that $z=3.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y -(3) = 2 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	y = 5.
$$

Now, we substitute both $y=5$ and $z=3$ into the first equation to get

$$
x + 2(5) + (3) = 1
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x = -12.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-12,$ $y=5,$ and $z=3.$ We can write it in vector form, as follows:

$$
\left\langle -12,5,3 \right\rangle = 
	\begin{bmatrix}-12 \\ 5 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

**Note:** The values $x=-12,$ $y=5,$ and $z=3$ together form *one* solution. We say that this system has *one* solution, *not* three solutions. A system with three solutions would have three different solution vectors, whereas here, we only have *one* solution vector.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=3 \\ y+z &=2 \\ z &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The third equation states that $z=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(2)=2 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	y = 2-2 = 0.
$$

Now, we substitute both $z=2$ and $y=0$ into the first equation to get

$$
x+(0)+(2)=3
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x = 3-2 = 1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x = 1,$ $y=0,$ and $z = 2.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 1,0,2 \rangle.$

$$

Now, we substitute ${x}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}$ and ${x}_{3}=2$ into the first equation to get

Therefore, the solution is ${x}_{1}=\frac{5}{2}$, ${x}_{2}=\frac{5}{2}$, and ${x}_{3}=2.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨\frac{5}{2},\frac{5}{2},2⟩.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a System of Equations Using Back Substitution

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations that is represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{array} 
	\right].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ {x}_{3} &=5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that $x_3=5.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(5)=-2
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_2=-2-5=-7.
$$

Now, we substitute both $x_3 = 5$ and $x_2 = -7$ into the first equation to get

$$
x_1+(-7)-(5) = 1
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_1 = 1 + 7 + 5 = 13.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x_1 = 13,$ $x_2=-7,$ and $x_3 = 5.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 13,-7,5 \rangle.$

$$

The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x$, $y$, and $z.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=1 \\ z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that $z=1.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(1)=1\,⟹\,y=1-1=0.
$$

Now, we substitute $z=1$ and $y=0$ into the first equation to get

$$
x+(0)+(1)=1\,⟹\,x=1-1=0.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=0$, $y=0$, and $z=1.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨0,0,1⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations that is represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}2 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 3\end{array} 
	\right].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ 3{x}_{3} &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that

$$
3x_3=3 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
	x_3=1.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(1)=-2
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_2=-2-1=-3.
$$

Now, we substitute both $x_3 = 1$ and $x_2 = -3$ into the first equation to get

$$
2x_1+(-3)-(1) = 0
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} (3 + 1) = 2.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x_1 = 2,$ $x_2=-3,$ and $x_3 = 1.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 2,-3,1 \rangle.$

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=3$, $y=-1$, and $z=0.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨3,-1,0⟩.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x$, $y$, and $z.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y+z &=-1 \\ y+z &=1 \\ 2z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that
 

$$
2z=1\,⟹\,z=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(\frac{1}{2})=1\,⟹\,y=1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.

Now, we substitute $z=y=\frac{1}{2}$  into the first equation to get

$$
2x+(\frac{1}{2})+(\frac{1}{2})=-1\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{2}(-1-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})=-1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-1$, $y=\frac{1}{2}$, and $z=\frac{1}{2}.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨-1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the system of equations that is represented by the augmented matrix

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{array} 
	\right].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=1 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ {x}_{3} &=5\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that $x_3=5.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(5)=-2
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_2=-2-5=-7.
$$

Now, we substitute both $x_3 = 5$ and $x_2 = -7$ into the first equation to get

$$
x_1+(-7)-(5) = 1
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_1 = 1 + 7 + 5 = 13.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x_1 = 13,$ $x_2=-7,$ and $x_3 = 5.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 13,-7,5 \rangle.$

$$
x+(0)+(1)=1\,⟹\,x=1-1=0.

$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The matrix represents a system of three linear equations in three variables, say, $x_1,$ $x_2,$ and $x_3.$ We obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ 3{x}_{3} &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that

$$
3x_3=3 
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
	x_3=1.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
x_2+(1)=-2
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_2=-2-1=-3.
$$

Now, we substitute both $x_3 = 1$ and $x_2 = -3$ into the first equation to get

$$
2x_1+(-3)-(1) = 0
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	x_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} (3 + 1) = 2.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x_1 = 2,$ $x_2=-3,$ and $x_3 = 1.$ Or, in vector form, the solution is $\langle 2,-3,1 \rangle.$

 Substituting this into the second equation, we get

-z=2\,⟹\,z=-2.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

3y+2(-2)=-1\,⟹\,y=\frac{1}{3}(-1+4)=1.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y+z &=-1 \\ y+z &=1 \\ 2z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The third equation states that
 

$$
2z=1\,⟹\,z=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
y+(\frac{1}{2})=1\,⟹\,y=1-\frac{1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}.

Now, we substitute $z=y=\frac{1}{2}$  into the first equation to get

$$
2x+(\frac{1}{2})+(\frac{1}{2})=-1\,⟹\,x=\frac{1}{2}(-1-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2})=-1.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-1$, $y=\frac{1}{2}$, and $z=\frac{1}{2}.$ In vector form, the solution can be written as $⟨-1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}⟩.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Remember that we can represent a system of two linear equations in two variables using matrices. We can do the same thing for a system of three linear equations in three variables, such as the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y\text{ }-\text{ }2z &=7 \\ 2x\text{ }-\text{ }1y\text{ }-\text{ }4z &=2 \\ 2x+1y\text{ }-\text{ }3z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

For a $3 \times 3$ system like the one above, we put the coefficients of the system into a $3 \times 3$ coefficient matrix:

![](images/40/40541d2ecb10c763056ae72734e723a9d5967ed9accaf0bbde6f2a2f9ec96b65.svg)

Each row has the coefficients of one of the equations in the system, and each column consists of the coefficients of one particular variable.
We also have the $3 \times 1$ column vectors

![](images/e5/e56ed72d2d17f9a4bc59bfe51a96534a72ebe481a312b8e9c6c028ade96d3748.svg)

where $\mathbf{b}$ consists of each constant on the right side of the system and $\mathbf{x}$ contains the variables.
With these matrices, we can write our system as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ or

![](images/f0/f06e5a54e106bcdca8b5cbad677ade3476ba8f6218b4aa79d196f54e0fff3e2c.svg)

We can write any system of three equations with three variables in this form. Just to check that the above equation is true, let's multiply out the left-hand side to see if it equals the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3x+2y\text{ }-\text{ }2z \\ 2x\text{ }-\text{ }1y\text{ }-\text{ }4z \\ 2x+1y\text{ }-\text{ }3z\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =b\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
The system of equations

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}6x+4y &=1 \\ x-8y-z &=-2 \\ 3x+2y-2z &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

can be represented using matrix notation as

![](images/21/212a3beac5ede3786bad835a693b0a725f331de41d6969dce7f17925dde012d7.svg)

What are the values of $a,$ $b$ and $c?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's write the system so that $x$, $y$, and $z$ appear in each equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}6x+4y+0z &=1 \\ x-8y-z &=-2 \\ 3x+2y-2z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can write the system in the form $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ where

![](images/22/22034036ec7859b56e9e19124e33fa616eddfc3784e15f8074583e28253a4bae.svg)

is the coefficient matrix,

![](images/b5/b5e0f47e7c4bb15e8923bceb665dcc87944090e3a39f9a335b17ab0b85025cc8.svg)

is the column vector of constants, and

![](images/b6/b643463daef16c2179d6f6320d31353a23b042f3774295eb55e48af0242ec655.svg)

is the column vector of variables.

So, the equation $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ becomes

![](images/bf/bf8fb79fd8998c5c867fc371535e26f2e92bea5fa7262789bd44aea07e24f93c.svg)

Therefore, $a=6,$ $b=2,$ and $c=-2.$

The system of equations

\left\{\begin{aligned}3x-4y+z &=2 \\ x-6y+11z &=3 \\ 3x-4y-z &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

can be represented using matrix notation as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 & a \\ 1 & b & c \\ 3 & -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

What are the values of $a,b$ and $c?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We can write the system in the form $Ax=b,$ where

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & -6 & 11 \\ 3 & -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}
$$

is the coefficient matrix,

$$
b=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

is the column vector of constants, and

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}
$$

is the column vector of variables.

So, the equation $Ax=b$ becomes

$$
\begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 & 1 \\ 1 & -6 & 11 \\ 3 & -4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, $a=1,\,b=-6,\,c=11.$

The system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+2z &=0 \\ x+2y+3z &=2 \\ 3x+y+z &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

can be represented using matrix notation as

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & a & 2 \\ b & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & c\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

What are the values of $a,b$ and $c?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's write the system so that $x$, $y$, and $z$ appear in each equation:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}0x+y+2z &=0 \\ x+2y+3z &=2 \\ 3x+y+z &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we can write the system in the form $Ax=b,$ where

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

is the coefficient matrix,

$$
b=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}
$$

is the column vector of constants, and

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}
$$

is the column vector of variables.

So, the equation $Ax=b$ becomes

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, $a=1,\,b=1,\,c=1.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Entries of a Matrix Product Representing a 3x3 System of Equations by Reorganizing

17592186049151.:topic/title: Representing 3x3 Systems of Equations Using a Matrix Product

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Remember that we can represent a system of two linear equations in two variables using matrices. We can do the same thing for a system of three linear equations in three variables, such as the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y\text{ }-\text{ }2z &=7 \\ 2x\text{ }-\text{ }1y\text{ }-\text{ }4z &=2 \\ 2x+1y\text{ }-\text{ }3z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

For a $3 \times 3$ system like the one above, we put the coefficients of the system into a $3 \times 3$ coefficient matrix:

![](images/40/40541d2ecb10c763056ae72734e723a9d5967ed9accaf0bbde6f2a2f9ec96b65.svg)

Each row has the coefficients of one of the equations in the system, and each column consists of the coefficients of one particular variable.
We also have the $3 \times 1$ column vectors

![](images/e5/e56ed72d2d17f9a4bc59bfe51a96534a72ebe481a312b8e9c6c028ade96d3748.svg)

where $\mathbf{b}$ consists of each constant on the right side of the system and $\mathbf{x}$ contains the variables.
With these matrices, we can write our system as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ or

![](images/f0/f06e5a54e106bcdca8b5cbad677ade3476ba8f6218b4aa79d196f54e0fff3e2c.svg)

We can write any system of three equations with three variables in this form. Just to check that the above equation is true, let's multiply out the left-hand side to see if it equals the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3x+2y\text{ }-\text{ }2z \\ 2x\text{ }-\text{ }1y\text{ }-\text{ }4z \\ 2x+1y\text{ }-\text{ }3z\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =b\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
