:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Remember that we can represent a system of two linear equations in two variables using matrices. We can do the same thing for a system of three linear equations in three variables, such as the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y\text{ }-\text{ }2z &=7 \\ 2x\text{ }-\text{ }1y\text{ }-\text{ }4z &=2 \\ 2x+1y\text{ }-\text{ }3z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

For a $3 \times 3$ system like the one above, we put the coefficients of the system into a $3 \times 3$ coefficient matrix:

![](images/40/40541d2ecb10c763056ae72734e723a9d5967ed9accaf0bbde6f2a2f9ec96b65.svg)

Each row has the coefficients of one of the equations in the system, and each column consists of the coefficients of one particular variable.
We also have the $3 \times 1$ column vectors

![](images/e5/e56ed72d2d17f9a4bc59bfe51a96534a72ebe481a312b8e9c6c028ade96d3748.svg)

where $\mathbf{b}$ consists of each constant on the right side of the system and $\mathbf{x}$ contains the variables.
With these matrices, we can write our system as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ or

![](images/f0/f06e5a54e106bcdca8b5cbad677ade3476ba8f6218b4aa79d196f54e0fff3e2c.svg)

We can write any system of three equations with three variables in this form. Just to check that the above equation is true, let's multiply out the left-hand side to see if it equals the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & -2 \\ 2 & -1 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3x+2y\text{ }-\text{ }2z \\ 2x\text{ }-\text{ }1y\text{ }-\text{ }4z \\ 2x+1y\text{ }-\text{ }3z\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =b\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We know that we can write a system of three linear equations in three variables in the form $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where

- $A$ is the $3\times 3$ coefficient matrix,

- $\mathbf{x}$ is the column vector of variables, and

- $\mathbf{b}$ is the column vector of constants.

If the $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ is invertible, then we can find a solution to the system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by "pre-multiplying" both sides of the equation by $A^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ {A}^{-1}Ax & ={A}^{-1}b \\ {I}_{3}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\ x & ={A}^{-1}b\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ we simply calculate $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$

Let's see how this works for a particular system in the next example.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x+5y-2z &=-2 \\ -3y+z &=-2 \\ 3x-7y+3z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The system above has the matrix representation $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.$ Given that $\mathbf x = \langle x,y,z\rangle$ is unique, what is the value of $x+y+z?$ 

*Hint: The inverse of the coefficient matrix is given by*
![](images/22/220e8838850356768215ed74aefc469edbdc99aa50b9116729329f0e818d6978.svg)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's write our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -7 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 9 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution is $x=3, y=0, z=-2.$

Finally, $x+y+z=3+0+(-2)=1.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Given the Inverse of the Coefficient Matrix

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations using matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}3y+x+z &=0 \\ z+4y-5 &=2 \\ 1+2x-y &=-3\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we organize the system so that the variables are in the correct order and every variable has a coefficient:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}x+3y+z &=0 \\ 0x+4y+z &=7 \\ 2x-y+0z &=-4\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

![](images/e8/e816a0fcde823bc6f6e88dff0a02c1877275cbed75757c1eb366fb224629127e.svg)

Now, the solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$ So, we compute $A^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1*: Find the determinant of $A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)-3(-2)+(-8) \\  & =1+6-8 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2*: Compute the matrix of minors.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & -7 \\ -1 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3*:  Find the matrix of cofactors.

![](images/be/beb80ea3185fc723c294313b63274554ec8af3531ed5643173a6127c59a21bb3.svg)

*Step 4*: Transpose the matrix of cofactors.

![](images/e6/e6fac5dd0a9918a03ce7c14e9cd05a06c6d11e95346f261ec75d6ebea09de1d6.svg)

*Step 5*: Apply the inverse matrix formula.

![](images/72/72b9d627d372d7a64a271b555b0d4cbb89b2bf9d602cdec64b1d8987a5e21521.svg)

Finally, we can calculate the solution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 8 & -7 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 10 \\ -33\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=3,$ $y=10,$ $z=-33.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3+z &=0 \\ 5y-1+3x &=2z+1 \\ 3z+2x-1 &=2y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+z &=3 \\ 3x+5y-2z &=2 \\ 2x-2y+3z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-0+\begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(15-4)+(-6-10) \\  & =22-16 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 5\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}11 & 13 & -16 \\ 2 & 4 & -4 \\ -5 & -7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -13 & -16 \\ -2 & 4 & 4 \\ -5 & 7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}24 \\ -24 \\ -30\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -4 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $x+y+z=4-4-5=-5.$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+3z &=-1 \\ y+4z &=1 \\ 5x+6y &=0\end{aligned}\right.

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-24)-2(-20)+3(-5) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-24 & -20 & -5 \\ -18 & -15 & -4 \\ 5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 20 & -5 \\ 18 & -15 & 4 \\ 5 & -4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}42 \\ -35 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+3z &=-1 \\ 4y+5z &=0 \\ x+6z &=3\end{aligned}\right.

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3z-y+x-5 &=0 \\ y+2x+2z &=1 \\ z-2x-2y &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+3z &=5 \\ 2x+y+2z &=1 \\ -2x-2y+z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 & 3 \\ 2 & 1 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}-(-1)\begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(1+4)+1(2+4)+3(-4+2) \\  & =5+6-6 \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

*Step 2:*

$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-2(2)+2(1) \\  & =-4+2 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 8 \\ -7\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{2} \\ 4 \\ -\frac{7}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+z &=1 \\ 2x-2z &=2+2y \\ 2y+4z &=2x-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+z &=1 \\ 2x-2y-2z &=2 \\ -2x+2y+4z &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-(8-4)+(4-4) \\  & =-4+0 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -4 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{-4}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=2+1+0=3.$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

$$

$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 6 & -2 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 & -4 \\ -6 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$

\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -3 & 3 \\ -1 & 4 & -7 \\ 1 & 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 7 \\ 1 & -5 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & -5 \\ 3 & 7 & -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 9 \\ 18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+2z &=0 \\ x+2y+3z &=2 \\ 3x+y+z &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2},y=9,z=-\frac{9}{2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z &=-1 \\ 3x-z &=5+3y \\ 3z-2y &=6-x\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z &=-1 \\ 3x-3y-z &=5 \\ x-2y+3z &=6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(-9-2)-(9+1)-2(-6+3) \\  & =-22-10+6 \\  & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -3\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 10 & -3 \\ -1 & 8 & -5 \\ -7 & 4 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-11 & -10 & -3 \\ 1 & 8 & 5 \\ -7 & -4 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-26 \\ 26 \\ -26\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=1-1+1=1.$

:step/content.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+2z &=0 \\ x+2y+3z &=2 \\ 3x+y+z &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:step/content.:question/worked-solution:
We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2},y=9,z=-\frac{9}{2}.$

From top to bottom and right to left, what are the missing parts of the derivation?
:step/content.:question/worked-solution:
Since $D$ is not singular, it must have an inverse ${D}^{-1}.$ Now, pre-multiplying both sides of the equation $D\,z=c$ by ${D}^{-1},$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,z & =c \\ {D}^{-1}D\,z & ={D}^{-1}c \\ {I}_{n}\,z & ={D}^{-1}\,c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts are ${D}^{-1}$ and ${I}_{n}.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x+5y-2z &=-2 \\ -3y+z &=-2 \\ 3x-7y+3z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The system above has the matrix representation $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.$ Given that $\mathbf x = \langle x,y,z\rangle$ is unique, what is the value of $x+y+z?$ 

*Hint: The inverse of the coefficient matrix is given by*
![](images/22/220e8838850356768215ed74aefc469edbdc99aa50b9116729329f0e818d6978.svg)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's write our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -7 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 9 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution is $x=3, y=0, z=-2.$

Finally, $x+y+z=3+0+(-2)=1.$

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Given the Inverse of the Coefficient Matrix

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations using matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}3y+x+z &=0 \\ z+4y-5 &=2 \\ 1+2x-y &=-3\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we organize the system so that the variables are in the correct order and every variable has a coefficient:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}x+3y+z &=0 \\ 0x+4y+z &=7 \\ 2x-y+0z &=-4\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

![](images/e8/e816a0fcde823bc6f6e88dff0a02c1877275cbed75757c1eb366fb224629127e.svg)

Now, the solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$ So, we compute $A^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1*: Find the determinant of $A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)-3(-2)+(-8) \\  & =1+6-8 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2*: Compute the matrix of minors.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & -7 \\ -1 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3*:  Find the matrix of cofactors.

![](images/be/beb80ea3185fc723c294313b63274554ec8af3531ed5643173a6127c59a21bb3.svg)

*Step 4*: Transpose the matrix of cofactors.

![](images/e6/e6fac5dd0a9918a03ce7c14e9cd05a06c6d11e95346f261ec75d6ebea09de1d6.svg)

*Step 5*: Apply the inverse matrix formula.

![](images/72/72b9d627d372d7a64a271b555b0d4cbb89b2bf9d602cdec64b1d8987a5e21521.svg)

Finally, we can calculate the solution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 8 & -7 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 10 \\ -33\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=3,$ $y=10,$ $z=-33.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3+z &=0 \\ 5y-1+3x &=2z+1 \\ 3z+2x-1 &=2y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+z &=3 \\ 3x+5y-2z &=2 \\ 2x-2y+3z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-0+\begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(15-4)+(-6-10) \\  & =22-16 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 5\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}11 & 13 & -16 \\ 2 & 4 & -4 \\ -5 & -7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -13 & -16 \\ -2 & 4 & 4 \\ -5 & 7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$

$$

*Step 2:*

$$

$$

$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$

$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ -2 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}-1 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & 7 & -4 \\ -5 & -4 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

*Step 3:*

$$

*Step 4:*

$$

Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+z &=1 \\ 2x-2z &=2+2y \\ 2y+4z &=2x-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+z &=1 \\ 2x-2y-2z &=2 \\ -2x+2y+4z &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-(8-4)+(4-4) \\  & =-4+0 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -4 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{-4}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=2+1+0=3.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$

$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=2 \\ y-3z &=3 \\ 2x+y+4z &=4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 \\ 2 & 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4+3)-(0+6)+(0-2) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & -3 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & 6 & -2 \\ 3 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -6 & -2 \\ -3 & 2 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & 1\text{ }\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 & -4 \\ -6 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}7 & -3 & -4 \\ -6 & 2 & 3 \\ -2 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 3 & 4 \\ 6 & -2 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-7 & 3 & 4 \\ 6 & -2 & -3 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}11 \\ -6 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=11,y=-6,z=-3.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}z+x &=2 \\ 2y-3z &=1 \\ 2z-y &=-3x+3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+z &=2 \\ 2y-3z &=1 \\ 3x-y+2z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4-3)-0+(0-6) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 9 & -6 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 & -6 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=1,y=2,z=1.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}y+2z &=0 \\ x+2y+3z &=2 \\ 3x+y+z &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 3 & 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix}+2\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-1(1-9)+2(1-6) \\  & =+8-10 \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -8 & -5 \\ -1 & -6 & -3 \\ -1 & -2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 8 & -5 \\ 1 & -6 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & 2 \\ -5 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 \\ -8 & 6 & -2 \\ 5 & -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-\frac{5}{2} \\ 9 \\ -\frac{9}{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

Hence the solution is $x=-\frac{5}{2},y=9,z=-\frac{9}{2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z &=-1 \\ 3x-z &=5+3y \\ 3z-2y &=6-x\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z &=-1 \\ 3x-3y-z &=5 \\ x-2y+3z &=6\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix}+(-2)\begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(-9-2)-(9+1)-2(-6+3) \\  & =-22-10+6 \\  & =-26.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-3 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 1 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 \\ -3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -3\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 10 & -3 \\ -1 & 8 & -5 \\ -7 & 4 & -9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-11 & -10 & -3 \\ 1 & 8 & 5 \\ -7 & -4 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-11 & 1 & -7 \\ -10 & 8 & -4 \\ -3 & 5 & -9\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-\frac{1}{26}\begin{bmatrix}-26 \\ 26 \\ -26\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=1-1+1=1.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Consider a matrix equation $B\,\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\,\mathbf{d},$ where $A$ and $B$ are $10 \times 10$ non-singular matrices, while $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ are $10 \times 1$ column vectors. Solve the equation for $\mathbf{x}.$

$$

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Consider a matrix equation $AB\,x=d,$ where $A$ and $B$ are $4\times 4$ non-singular matrices, while $x$ and $d$ are $4\times 1$ column vectors. Solve the equation for $x.$

Since $A$ is not singular, it must have an inverse ${A}^{-1}.$ Now, pre-multiplying both sides of the equation $AB\,x=d$ by ${A}^{-1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}AB\,x & =d \\ {A}^{-1}AB\,x & ={A}^{-1}\,d \\ {I}_{4}B\,x & ={A}^{-1}\,d \\ B\,x & ={A}^{-1}\,d.\end{aligned}

Since $B$ is not singular, it must have an inverse ${B}^{-1}.$ Now, pre-multiplying both sides of the equation $B\,x={A}^{-1}\,d$ by ${B}^{-1},$ we obtain

Now, pre-multiplying both sides of the equation ${B}^{-1}\,x=A\,d$ by $B,$ we obtain

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Consider a matrix equation $A{B}^{-1}\,x=d,$ where $A$ and $B$ are $5\times 5$ non-singular matrices, while $x$ and $d$ are $5\times 1$ column vectors. Solve the equation for $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,z & =c \\ {D}^{-1}D\,z & =\bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{{D}^{-1}}}}c \\ \bbox[2pt,lightgray]{\color{blue}{\phantom{{I}_{n}}}}z & ={D}^{-1}\,c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Since $D$ is not singular, it must have an inverse ${D}^{-1}.$ Now, pre-multiplying both sides of the equation $D\,z=c$ by ${D}^{-1},$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}D\,z & =c \\ {D}^{-1}D\,z & ={D}^{-1}c \\ {I}_{n}\,z & ={D}^{-1}\,c \\ z & ={D}^{-1}\,c\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the missing parts are ${D}^{-1}$ and ${I}_{n}.$

Some linear equations have **infinitely many solutions.** 

For example, consider the following equation: 

$$
x+5 = x + 5
$$

Let's attempt to solve this equation by subtracting $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\ x+5-x & =x+5-x \\ 5 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

So, what does $x$ equal? The statement $5=5$ is *always* true, irrespective of the value of $x.$ This tells us that *any* value of $x$ is a solution to the equation!

Don't believe it? If we substitute any value, say $x=3,$ into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\ 3+5 & =3+5 \\ 8 & =8.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

It's important to note that substituting *any* value for $x$ into the equation will lead to a true statement. For example, the values 

$$
x=42,\qquad x=-\dfrac 1 4, \qquad x=1.2345
$$

are *all* solutions to the original equation.

To summarize:

- Our original equation has *infinitely many solutions.*

- The solution of the equation is "*any (real) value of* $x$".

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$

II. $-3x = -4x + 6$

III. $2x + 7 = 2x - 1$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+1 & =4x+1 \\ 4x+1-4x & =4x+1-4x \\ 1 & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x & =-4x+6 \\ -3x+4x & =-4x+6+4x \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $-3x = -4x + 6$ has the unique solution $x = 6.$

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+7 & =2x-1 \\ 2x+7-2x & =2x-1-2x \\ 7 & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+1 & =2x+1 \\ 2x+1-2x & =2x+1-2x \\ 1 & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $2x+1=2x+1$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+1 & =2x+3 \\ 2x+1-2x & =2x+3-2x \\ 1 & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Equations With Infinitely Many Solutions

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax = bx,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a = b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.

For example, each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x=2x,\,\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{1}{3}x\,-2.16x=-2.16x\end{aligned}
$$

To show that the general equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ we can substitute $a$ for $b$ in our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =bx \\ ax & =(a)x \\ ax & =ax\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we simplify this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =ax \\ ax-ax & =ax-ax \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The equation, $0=0,$ is always true, regardless of the value of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ and any value of $x$ is a solution to the equation.

Consider the equation

$$
2qx = 10x,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. If we're given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = bx{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{2q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{10}_{\large b} \ x
$$

In this case, 

$$
a = 2q, \qquad b = 10.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b.$ Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
2q = 10.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =10 \\ \frac{2q}{2} & =\frac{10}{2} \\ q & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2qx = 10x$ has infinitely many solutions if $q = 5.$

We can check that this answer is correct by substituting $q = 5$ into our original equation. Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\ 2(5)x & =10x \\ 10x & =10x\end{aligned}
$$

and simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $x.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
2x + 1 = 2x + 1, \qquad \dfrac13x -2 = \dfrac13x -2, \qquad 1-x = 1 - x
$$

More generally, suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax + b = cx + d,
$$

where $a, b, c,$ and $d$ are constants. Then, this equation has infinitely many solutions if 

$$
a = c\quad \text{and}\quad b = d.
$$

Note that if we substitute $c=a$ and $d=b$ into this equation, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =cx+d \\ ax+b & =(a)x+(b) \\ ax+b & =ax+b\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =ax+b \\ ax+b-ax & =ax+b-ax \\ b & =b\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation, $b = b,$ is always true. Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions, and any real value of $x$ is a solution.

Consider the equation

$$
(s - 2)x + t = 6x + 9,
$$

where $s$ and $t$ are constants. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the values of $s$ and $t?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax+b = cx+d{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{(s-2)}_{\large a} \ x + \underbrace{t}_{\large b} = \underbrace{6}_{\large c} \ x + \underbrace{9}_{\large d}
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax+b = cx+d$ has infinitely many solutions when $a=c$ and $b=d.$

So, to determine the values of $s$ and $t$ such that the equation

$$
({\color{blue}{{s - 2}}})x + {\color{red}{{t}}} = {\color{blue}{{6}}}x + {\color{red}{{9}}}
$$

has infinitely many solutions, we **equate the coefficients** of $x,$ and we **equate the constants:**

- Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we have

$$
{\color{blue}{{s - 2}}} = {\color{blue}{{6}}}.
$$

Solving this equation for $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Equating the constants, we get

$$
{\color{red}{{t}}} = {\color{red}{{9}}}.
$$

Therefore, if $s = 8$ and $t=9,$ our original equation has infinitely many solutions.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$

II. $-3x = -4x + 6$

III. $2x + 7 = 2x - 1$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+1 & =4x+1 \\ 4x+1-4x & =4x+1-4x \\ 1 & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x & =-4x+6 \\ -3x+4x & =-4x+6+4x \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $-3x = -4x + 6$ has the unique solution $x = 6.$

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+7 & =2x-1 \\ 2x+7-2x & =2x-1-2x \\ 7 & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

$$
k + r = 2+4 = 6.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Some linear equations have **infinitely many solutions.** 

For example, consider the following equation: 

$$
x+5 = x + 5
$$

Let's attempt to solve this equation by subtracting $x$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\ x+5-x & =x+5-x \\ 5 & =5\end{aligned}
$$

So, what does $x$ equal? The statement $5=5$ is *always* true, irrespective of the value of $x.$ This tells us that *any* value of $x$ is a solution to the equation!

Don't believe it? If we substitute any value, say $x=3,$ into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+5 & =x+5 \\ 3+5 & =3+5 \\ 8 & =8.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

It's important to note that substituting *any* value for $x$ into the equation will lead to a true statement. For example, the values 

$$
x=42,\qquad x=-\dfrac 1 4, \qquad x=1.2345
$$

are *all* solutions to the original equation.

To summarize:

- Our original equation has *infinitely many solutions.*

- The solution of the equation is "*any (real) value of* $x$".

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following equations has infinitely many solutions?

I. $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$

II. $-3x = -4x + 6$

III. $2x + 7 = 2x - 1$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's attempt to solve each equation in turn:

- For the first equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+1 & =4x+1 \\ 4x+1-4x & =4x+1-4x \\ 1 & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $4x + 1 = 4x + 1$ has infinitely many solutions.

- For the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-3x & =-4x+6 \\ -3x+4x & =-4x+6+4x \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $-3x = -4x + 6$ has the unique solution $x = 6.$

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+7 & =2x-1 \\ 2x+7-2x & =2x-1-2x \\ 7 & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is false for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Equations With Infinitely Many Solutions

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax = bx,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a = b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.

For example, each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x=2x,\,\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{1}{3}x\,-2.16x=-2.16x\end{aligned}
$$

To show that the general equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ we can substitute $a$ for $b$ in our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =bx \\ ax & =(a)x \\ ax & =ax\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we simplify this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =ax \\ ax-ax & =ax-ax \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The equation, $0=0,$ is always true, regardless of the value of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ and any value of $x$ is a solution to the equation.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider the equation

$$
2qx = 10x,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. If we're given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = bx{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{2q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{10}_{\large b} \ x
$$

In this case, 

$$
a = 2q, \qquad b = 10.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b.$ Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
2q = 10.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =10 \\ \frac{2q}{2} & =\frac{10}{2} \\ q & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2qx = 10x$ has infinitely many solutions if $q = 5.$

We can check that this answer is correct by substituting $q = 5$ into our original equation. Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\ 2(5)x & =10x \\ 10x & =10x\end{aligned}
$$

and simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $x.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving For an Unknown Parameter

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
2x + 1 = 2x + 1, \qquad \dfrac13x -2 = \dfrac13x -2, \qquad 1-x = 1 - x
$$

More generally, suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax + b = cx + d,
$$

where $a, b, c,$ and $d$ are constants. Then, this equation has infinitely many solutions if 

$$
a = c\quad \text{and}\quad b = d.
$$

Note that if we substitute $c=a$ and $d=b$ into this equation, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =cx+d \\ ax+b & =(a)x+(b) \\ ax+b & =ax+b\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =ax+b \\ ax+b-ax & =ax+b-ax \\ b & =b\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation, $b = b,$ is always true. Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions, and any real value of $x$ is a solution.

Consider the equation

$$
(s - 2)x + t = 6x + 9,
$$

where $s$ and $t$ are constants. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the values of $s$ and $t?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax+b = cx+d{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{(s-2)}_{\large a} \ x + \underbrace{t}_{\large b} = \underbrace{6}_{\large c} \ x + \underbrace{9}_{\large d}
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax+b = cx+d$ has infinitely many solutions when $a=c$ and $b=d.$

So, to determine the values of $s$ and $t$ such that the equation

$$
({\color{blue}{{s - 2}}})x + {\color{red}{{t}}} = {\color{blue}{{6}}}x + {\color{red}{{9}}}
$$

has infinitely many solutions, we **equate the coefficients** of $x,$ and we **equate the constants:**

- Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we have

$$
{\color{blue}{{s - 2}}} = {\color{blue}{{6}}}.
$$

Solving this equation for $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Equating the constants, we get

$$
{\color{red}{{t}}} = {\color{red}{{9}}}.
$$

Therefore, if $s = 8$ and $t=9,$ our original equation has infinitely many solutions.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Some linear equations have **infinitely many solutions.** 

For example, consider the following equation: 

$$
x+5 = x + 5
$$

Let's attempt to solve this equation by subtracting $x$ from both sides:

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}6x+1 & =6x+9 \\ 6x+1-6x & =6x+9-6x \\ 1 & =9.\end{aligned}

- For the third equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x+3 & =-4x+3 \\ -4x+3+4x & =-4x+3+4x \\ 3 & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation is true for all values of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $-4x+3=-4x+3$ has infinitely many solutions.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax = bx,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants. If $a = b,$ then the equation has infinitely many solutions.

For example, each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x=2x,\,\frac{1}{3}x=\frac{1}{3}x\,-2.16x=-2.16x\end{aligned}
$$

To show that the general equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ we can substitute $a$ for $b$ in our equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =bx \\ ax & =(a)x \\ ax & =ax\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we simplify this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax & =ax \\ ax-ax & =ax-ax \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The equation, $0=0,$ is always true, regardless of the value of $x.$ Therefore, the equation $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b,$ and any value of $x$ is a solution to the equation.

Consider the equation

$$
2qx = 10x,
$$

where $q$ is a constant. If we're given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the value of $q?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax = bx{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{2q}_{\large a} \ x = \underbrace{10}_{\large b} \ x
$$

In this case, 

$$
a = 2q, \qquad b = 10.
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax = bx$ has infinitely many solutions whenever $a=b.$ Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions if

$$
2q = 10.
$$

Solving this for $q,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =10 \\ \frac{2q}{2} & =\frac{10}{2} \\ q & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation $2qx = 10x$ has infinitely many solutions if $q = 5.$

We can check that this answer is correct by substituting $q = 5$ into our original equation. Doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2qx & =10x \\ 2(5)x & =10x \\ 10x & =10x\end{aligned}
$$

and simplifying this equation by subtracting $10x$ from both sides yields

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & =10x \\ 10x-10x & =10x-10x \\ 0 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is true for all values of $x.$

**Note:** The constant $q$ in this problem is sometimes called a **parameter.**

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Each of the following equations has infinitely many solutions:

$$
2x + 1 = 2x + 1, \qquad \dfrac13x -2 = \dfrac13x -2, \qquad 1-x = 1 - x
$$

More generally, suppose we have an equation of the form

$$
ax + b = cx + d,
$$

where $a, b, c,$ and $d$ are constants. Then, this equation has infinitely many solutions if 

$$
a = c\quad \text{and}\quad b = d.
$$

Note that if we substitute $c=a$ and $d=b$ into this equation, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =cx+d \\ ax+b & =(a)x+(b) \\ ax+b & =ax+b\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation by subtracting $ax$ from both sides of the equation gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}ax+b & =ax+b \\ ax+b-ax & =ax+b-ax \\ b & =b\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation, $b = b,$ is always true. Therefore, the equation has infinitely many solutions, and any real value of $x$ is a solution.

Consider the equation

$$
(s - 2)x + t = 6x + 9,
$$

where $s$ and $t$ are constants. Given that this equation has infinitely many solutions, how can we find the values of $s$ and $t?$

Notice that this equation is in the form $ax+b = cx+d{:}$ 

$$
\underbrace{(s-2)}_{\large a} \ x + \underbrace{t}_{\large b} = \underbrace{6}_{\large c} \ x + \underbrace{9}_{\large d}
$$

We know that an equation of the form $ax+b = cx+d$ has infinitely many solutions when $a=c$ and $b=d.$

So, to determine the values of $s$ and $t$ such that the equation

$$
({\color{blue}{{s - 2}}})x + {\color{red}{{t}}} = {\color{blue}{{6}}}x + {\color{red}{{9}}}
$$

has infinitely many solutions, we **equate the coefficients** of $x,$ and we **equate the constants:**

- Equating the coefficients of $x,$ we have

$$
{\color{blue}{{s - 2}}} = {\color{blue}{{6}}}.
$$

Solving this equation for $s,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Equating the constants, we get

$$
{\color{red}{{t}}} = {\color{red}{{9}}}.
$$

Therefore, if $s = 8$ and $t=9,$ our original equation has infinitely many solutions.

$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We know that we can write a system of three linear equations in three variables in the form $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where

- $A$ is the $3\times 3$ coefficient matrix,

- $\mathbf{x}$ is the column vector of variables, and

- $\mathbf{b}$ is the column vector of constants.

If the $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ is invertible, then we can find a solution to the system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ by "pre-multiplying" both sides of the equation by $A^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ {A}^{-1}Ax & ={A}^{-1}b \\ {I}_{3}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\ x & ={A}^{-1}b\end{aligned}
$$

So, to find the solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ we simply calculate $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$

Let's see how this works for a particular system in the next example.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}-2x+5y-2z &=-2 \\ -3y+z &=-2 \\ 3x-7y+3z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The system above has the matrix representation $A \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.$ Given that $\mathbf x = \langle x,y,z\rangle$ is unique, what is the value of $x+y+z?$ 

*Hint: The inverse of the coefficient matrix is given by*
![](images/22/220e8838850356768215ed74aefc469edbdc99aa50b9116729329f0e818d6978.svg)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's write our system in matrix form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =b \\ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & 5 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -7 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 0 & 2 \\ 9 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution is $x=3, y=0, z=-2.$

Finally, $x+y+z=3+0+(-2)=1.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a 3x3 System of Equations Given the Inverse of the Coefficient Matrix

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations using matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}3y+x+z &=0 \\ z+4y-5 &=2 \\ 1+2x-y &=-3\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we organize the system so that the variables are in the correct order and every variable has a coefficient:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}x+3y+z &=0 \\ 0x+4y+z &=7 \\ 2x-y+0z &=-4\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

![](images/e8/e816a0fcde823bc6f6e88dff0a02c1877275cbed75757c1eb366fb224629127e.svg)

Now, the solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by $\mathbf{x}= A^{-1}\mathbf{b}.$ So, we compute $A^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1*: Find the determinant of $A.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 4 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & =1\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix}-3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(1)-3(-2)+(-8) \\  & =1+6-8 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2*: Compute the matrix of minors.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 4 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & -7 \\ -1 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3*:  Find the matrix of cofactors.

![](images/be/beb80ea3185fc723c294313b63274554ec8af3531ed5643173a6127c59a21bb3.svg)

*Step 4*: Transpose the matrix of cofactors.

![](images/e6/e6fac5dd0a9918a03ce7c14e9cd05a06c6d11e95346f261ec75d6ebea09de1d6.svg)

*Step 5*: Apply the inverse matrix formula.

![](images/72/72b9d627d372d7a64a271b555b0d4cbb89b2bf9d602cdec64b1d8987a5e21521.svg)

Finally, we can calculate the solution as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 1 \\ 8 & -7 & -4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 7 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 10 \\ -33\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=3,$ $y=10,$ $z=-33.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-3+z &=0 \\ 5y-1+3x &=2z+1 \\ 3z+2x-1 &=2y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Find  $x+y+z.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, let's rewrite the system in the correct order:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x+z &=3 \\ 3x+5y-2z &=2 \\ 2x-2y+3z &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix}-0+\begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2(15-4)+(-6-10) \\  & =22-16 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

 

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}5 & -2 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 3 & 5\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}11 & 13 & -16 \\ 2 & 4 & -4 \\ -5 & -7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -13 & -16 \\ -2 & 4 & 4 \\ -5 & 7 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the solution to the given system is

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}11 & -2 & -5 \\ -13 & 4 & 7 \\ -16 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\begin{bmatrix}24 \\ -24 \\ -30\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -4 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $x+y+z=4-4-5=-5.$

Solve the following system of linear equations by finding the inverse of the coefficient matrix:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2y+3z+x &=-1 \\ 4z+y &=1 \\ 5x+6y-3 &=-3\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We organize the system so that it’s in the correct order first:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y+3z &=-1 \\ y+4z &=1 \\ 5x+6y &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix}-2\begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix}+3\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1(-24)-2(-20)+3(-5) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 4 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 6 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 5 & 0\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 6\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-24 & -20 & -5 \\ -18 & -15 & -4 \\ 5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 20 & -5 \\ 18 & -15 & 4 \\ 5 & -4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-24 & 18 & 5 \\ 20 & -15 & -4 \\ -5 & 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}42 \\ -35 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=42,y=-35,z=9.$

Hence

$$

*Step 2:*

$$

$$

Next, we  write the system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0-(8-4)+(4-4) \\  & =-4+0 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & -2 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 4\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ -2 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -4 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=\frac{1}{-4}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.

$$

$$

Therefore, $x+y+z=2+1+0=3.$

We wish to write this system in the form $Ax=b$, where $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and $x$ and $b$ are $3\times 1$ column vectors. We can do this as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Now, the solution to $Ax=b$ is given by $x={A}^{-1}b.$ So, we compute ${A}^{-1}$ as follows:

*Step 1:*

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix}-0\begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix}+1\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(4-3)-0+(0-6) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 2:*

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}\begin{vmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\ \begin{vmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -3\end{vmatrix} & \begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{vmatrix}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 9 & -6 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

*Step 3:*

$$
C=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -9 & -6 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 \\ -2 & 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 4:*

$$
{C}^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

*Step 5:*

$$
{A}^{-1}=\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T}=-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 

Hence

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -9 & -1 & 3 \\ -6 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence the solution is $x=1,y=2,z=1.$
